<explanation>
This project is a browser-based HTML5 game—a clone of the popular 2048 game—written entirely in JavaScript and styled with CSS/SCSS. Given its nature, the project’s architecture is relatively simple and front-end–focused, but it’s still beneficial to clearly illustrate its components and how they interact.

Below is a guide tailored to drawing the system design diagram of this 2048 clone:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • User Interface (index.html): The entry point that loads the game and presents the UI.
   • JavaScript Modules (located in the js/ directory):
  – game_manager.js: The central coordinator managing game state, moves, and overall game flow.
  – grid.js & tile.js: Represent the game board structure, responsible for grid operations, tile management, and game logic.
  – keyboard_input_manager.js: Captures user inputs (keyboard events and, as noted in the README, mobile swipes) and relays them to the game manager.
  – html_actuator.js: Handles DOM updates and renders the game state onto the page.
  – local_storage_manager.js: Manages saving and retrieving game state and best scores to/from the browser's local storage.
  – Additional polyfill files (animframe_polyfill.js, bind_polyfill.js, classlist_polyfill.js): Ensure compatibility across browsers.
   • Styling Components (style/ directory):
  – CSS/SCSS files (main.css, main.scss, helpers.scss): Define the look and feel of the game.
  – Fonts (in style/fonts/): Provide custom fonts to enhance design aesthetics.
   • Meta/Build/Contribution Files:
  – Files like .gitignore, CONTRIBUTING.md, Rakefile, LICENSE.txt provide project governance and build/maintenance support.

2. Determine the Relationships and Interactions:
   • When a user interacts with the game (e.g., presses an arrow key or performs a swipe), the keyboard_input_manager captures the event.
   • This input is sent to the game_manager, which updates the game state by manipulating grid.js and tile.js (i.e., moving tiles, merging, generating new tiles).
   • After processing the game state, game_manager invokes html_actuator to update the DOM (using index.html as the base layout).
   • The local_storage_manager is called to persist the game state and best score so that progress can be maintained across sessions.
   • Polyfills ensure that any potential browser-specific issues are prevented, guaranteeing consistency in animations and function bindings.

3. Important Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Separation of Concerns: Different modules handle specific tasks (input handling, game state, rendering, persistence).
   • Modular JavaScript: Each file in the js/ directory represents a modular piece of functionality.
   • Progressive Enhancement and Compatibility: Use of polyfills ensures the game works across a broad range of browsers.
   • MVC-like Flow (even if not formally an MVC framework):
  – Model: The game state and board structure represented by grid.js and tile.js.
  – Controller: Game_manager.js as the orchestrator.
  – View: html_actuator.js, which updates the presentation layer in the browser.

4. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines for This Project:
   • Since this is a single-page browser game, emphasize the clear division between the input layer, game logic, state management, and UI rendering.
   • Create boxes for each key component:
  – “User Interface (index.html)”
  – “Keyboard Input Manager (keyboard_input_manager.js)”
  – “Game Manager (game_manager.js)”
  – “Grid & Tile Modules (grid.js, tile.js)”
  – “HTML Actuator (html_actuator.js)”
  – “Local Storage Manager (local_storage_manager.js)”
  – “Polyfills (animframe_polyfill.js, bind_polyfill.js, classlist_polyfill.js)”
  – “Styling (CSS/SCSS & Fonts)”
   • Draw directional arrows:
  – From the UI capturing user interactions to the Keyboard Input Manager.
  – From the Keyboard Input Manager to the Game Manager.
  – From the Game Manager to the Grid/Tile Modules (representing game state changes).
  – From the Game Manager to the HTML Actuator (for re-rendering the view).
  – From the Game Manager to the Local Storage Manager (for persistence).
   • Use color coding or distinct shapes:
  – For example, use one color for core game logic modules, another for utility modules (polyfills, storage) and yet another for presentation/styling.
   • Clearly label each component so anyone reviewing the diagram can quickly understand the module responsibilities and interdependencies.

5. Additional Considerations:
   • Even though the project is relatively compact, it’s important to capture all interactions to avoid ambiguity—especially because improvements or contributions might extend functionality (like mobile swipe enhancements).
   • Highlight any dependencies (for instance, how local storage functions as an external dependency for persistence even though it’s part of the browser).

By following these guidelines, you’ll generate a detailed and accurate high-level system design diagram. This diagram will clearly represent how user actions translate into game logic execution, UI rendering, and persistence within this 2048 clone. Remember that clarity and comprehensive labeling are key, as they ensure that every component and interaction is explicitly documented for future maintainers or contributors.
</explanation>
